sentences: Combining 321 SPHEREx pictures along a known path recovers planted test objects half the time down to visual magnitude 20.5 (measured).
This assumes we already know where the object moves. Searching for an unknown object means testing many possible paths, which raises the bar for a believable detection; that search is not done here.

Planted objects are grey (equally reflective at all colours). Most real asteroids are redder, so they look brighter to SPHEREx than their visual magnitude suggests: two real asteroids near magnitude 20.9 and 21.5 were detected by stacking (see the reveal).
Reflected sunlight only: a planet that glows from its own internal heat could be brighter in SPHEREx's longest colours than shown.
A Pluto-sized world (2,400 km), bright icy surface, at 100 au: about magnitude 19.2 — bright enough for a SPHEREx stack, if its path were known.
An Earth-sized planet (12,742 km), albedo 0.5, at 250 au: about magnitude 19.8 — bright enough for a SPHEREx stack, if its path were known.
A planet four times Earth's width (51,000 km), albedo 0.5, at 500 au: about magnitude 19.8 — bright enough for a SPHEREx stack, if its path were known.
The same planet at 700 au: about magnitude 21.3 — too faint for a SPHEREx stack.
Very bright planted objects are not a test of SPHEREx: real detectors saturate near magnitude 10–11.5, which the planted objects do not model.
